scenes.visual: Title card 'Which Side Grows Faster?' over a cartoon oat seedling leaning toward a BLUE light arrow. COLOUR MAP, same in both films and the lesson figures: auxin = GOLD dots (a GOLD band where it piles up); light = BLUE arrow; lit flank PALE GREEN; shaded flank WARM ORANGE; gravity = GREY down-arrow; PIN carriers = small TEAL gates on cell faces; starch statoliths = dark BROWN grains. Seedlings are simple cartoons, cream background, 16:9. Every number and date appears only as on-screen text. Anything not computed is labelled 'schematic'.

scenes.tts: Light an oat seedling from one side, and it bends toward the lamp. The tip senses the light, yet the bend forms lower down. What carries the message?
scenes.visual: A lamp at left sends a BLUE arrow at a straight seedling. Over a few seconds the seedling curves toward the lamp. The tip pulses with a small 'senses light' tag; a bracket lower down reads 'bends here'. A question mark travels between the two labels.
scenes.narration: Light an oat seedling from one side, and it bends toward the lamp. The tip senses the light, yet the bend forms lower down. What carries the message?

scenes.tts: Picture the young shoot as two columns of cells, one on each side. Each side is called a flank.
scenes.visual: The seedling zooms in and splits into two vertical columns of brick-like cells: left column PALE GREEN labelled 'lit flank', right column WARM ORANGE labelled 'shaded flank'. The word 'flank' writes itself between them.
scenes.narration: Picture the young shoot as two columns of cells, one on each side. Each side is called a flank.

scenes.tts: If both flanks lengthen by the same amount, the shoot grows taller. But it stays perfectly straight, however much it grows.
scenes.visual: Both columns add cells at the same rate; the shoot rises straight up. A side tag: 'same growth on both flanks: no bend'. No auxin dots are shown in this scene.
scenes.narration: If both flanks lengthen by the same amount, the shoot grows taller. But it stays perfectly straight, however much it grows.

scenes.tts: Now let the shaded flank lengthen a little more than the lit flank. The shoot curves toward the light. A bend is simply a difference in growth.
scenes.visual: The WARM ORANGE column stretches slightly more than the PALE GREEN one; the shoot curves toward the BLUE arrow. A small ruler on each flank shows the ORANGE one longer. Caption: 'bend = difference between flanks'.
scenes.narration: Now let the shaded flank lengthen a little more than the lit flank. The shoot curves toward the light. A bend is simply a difference in growth.

scenes.tts: So what speeds the shaded flank? Charles Darwin and his son Francis lit canary-grass seedlings from one side. An opaque cap over the tip greatly reduced the bending.
scenes.visual: Caption 'Charles and Francis Darwin, 1880'. Two canary-grass seedlings under a BLUE arrow: the bare one bends; one wearing a black cap on its tip stays almost straight, though the BLUE arrow still hits its lower part.
scenes.narration: So what speeds the shaded flank? Charles Darwin and his son Francis lit canary-grass seedlings from one side. An opaque cap over the tip greatly reduced the bending.

scenes.tts: The lower part was still lit. So light is sensed mainly near the tip, and something passes down to where bending happens.
scenes.visual: A highlight ring around the capped tip; a dotted arrow runs down the stem labelled 'something passes down?'.
scenes.narration: The lower part was still lit. So light is sensed mainly near the tip, and something passes down to where bending happens.

scenes.tts: Peter Boysen-Jensen used oat coleoptiles, the sheath over a grass seedling's first leaf. He slipped thin mica, which dissolved chemicals cannot cross, into a cut below the tip.
scenes.visual: Caption 'Peter Boysen-Jensen, oat, 1910 to 1913'. An oat coleoptile labelled 'coleoptile: sheath over the first leaf'. A thin silver sheet labelled 'mica' slides into a cut just below the tip, on one side.
scenes.narration: Peter Boysen-Jensen used oat coleoptiles, the sheath over a grass seedling's first leaf. He slipped thin mica, which dissolved chemicals cannot cross, into a cut below the tip.

scenes.tts: With mica on the shaded side, the coleoptile stayed straight. With mica on the lit side, it still bent. Boysen-Jensen concluded that the signal runs down the shaded side.
scenes.visual: Two coleoptiles side by side under a BLUE arrow. Left: mica on the WARM ORANGE shaded side, stays straight. Right: mica on the PALE GREEN lit side, bends. A dotted arrow runs down the shaded flank of the bent one.
scenes.narration: With mica on the shaded side, the coleoptile stayed straight. With mica on the lit side, it still bent. Boysen-Jensen concluded that the signal runs down the shaded side.

scenes.tts: Frits Went then stood cut tips on small blocks of agar, a gel. In darkness, he set one block on one side of a coleoptile whose own tip was cut off.
scenes.visual: Caption 'Frits Went, 1928'. Cut tips sit on a pale agar cube; GOLD dots drain from the tips into the gel. The scene darkens to night blue; the cube is placed on one side of a flat-topped, decapitated coleoptile.
scenes.narration: Frits Went then stood cut tips on small blocks of agar, a gel. In darkness, he set one block on one side of a coleoptile whose own tip was cut off.

scenes.tts: The coleoptile curved away from the block. Something from the tips had sped growth beneath it. We now call that activity auxin.
scenes.visual: GOLD dots flow from the cube down the flank beneath it; that flank lengthens and the coleoptile curves away from the block. A protractor measures the angle, label 'angle measures activity'. The word 'auxin' appears next to the GOLD dots.
scenes.narration: The coleoptile curved away from the block. Something from the tips had sped growth beneath it. We now call that activity auxin.

scenes.tts: Why does the shaded flank end up with more auxin? Light could destroy auxin on the lit side. Or light could move auxin across to the shaded side.
scenes.visual: Split screen of two lit tips full of GOLD dots. Left panel 'destroy': GOLD dots on the lit side fade away. Right panel 'move': GOLD dots slide across the tip to the shaded side. Both panels end with more GOLD on the shaded side.
scenes.narration: Why does the shaded flank end up with more auxin? Light could destroy auxin on the lit side. Or light could move auxin across to the shaded side.

scenes.tts: Here is the test. Collect all the auxin from tips lit on one side, and from tips kept dark. If light only moves auxin, how should the totals compare?
scenes.visual: Two jars labelled 'total from lit tips' and 'total from dark tips', empty, with a question card between them.
scenes.narration: Here is the test. Collect all the auxin from tips lit on one side, and from tips kept dark. If light only moves auxin, how should the totals compare?

scenes.visual: Predict pause. Question card holds; a 5-second ring timer counts down at bottom right.

scenes.tts: Briggs and colleagues split tips with a thin barrier and caught each half in its own block. Lit tips gave the same total as dark tips. But more came from the shaded half.
scenes.visual: Caption 'Briggs and colleagues, 1957'. A tip on two agar blocks, a thin barrier rising from the base but leaving the very top joined. GOLD dots fill the WARM ORANGE half's block more than the PALE GREEN half's. The two jars fill to the same level, label 'same total'. Block heights are schematic.
scenes.narration: Briggs and colleagues split tips with a thin barrier and caught each half in its own block. Lit tips gave the same total as dark tips. But more came from the shaded half.

scenes.tts: So in these grass tips, the unchanged total supports auxin moving to the shaded side, rather than being destroyed. The auxin-rich shaded flank grew faster, and the shoot bent toward the light.
scenes.visual: Back to the two-column shoot: GOLD dots cross the tip to the WARM ORANGE column, which lengthens more, and the shoot curves toward the BLUE arrow.
scenes.narration: So in these grass tips, the unchanged total supports auxin moving to the shaded side, rather than being destroyed. The auxin-rich shaded flank grew faster, and the shoot bent toward the light.

scenes.tts: Growth follows the auxin level, but not in strict proportion. It rises to a peak. Past that peak, more auxin slows growth.
scenes.visual: A small label pins to the seedling: 'measured in grass coleoptile tips'. Beside it a schematic curve of growth against auxin rises to a peak and then falls, labelled 'not proportional; falls past a peak (schematic)'. A small marker sits on the rising slope, labelled 'shaded flank here (assumed)'.
scenes.narration: Growth follows the auxin level, but not in strict proportion. It rises to a peak. Past that peak, more auxin slows growth.

scenes.tts: So a bend is a difference in growth. Light makes that difference by moving auxin to the shaded flank.
scenes.visual: Recap strip: equal columns (straight), unequal columns (bent), GOLD dots sliding to the WARM ORANGE flank.
scenes.narration: So a bend is a difference in growth. Light makes that difference by moving auxin to the shaded flank.

scenes.visual: End card with Hex. LINE: 'A bend is uneven growth: light shifts auxin to the shaded flank.'
